<reason>B built the decisive frame early: everything benign in PRO's case (supervised accounts, filters, time windows) is already allowed, so the motion's only novel content is "cannot easily bypass"—and that single feature is where every cost concentrates. B's fork (voluntary flag = the "suggestion" A itself called "no rule"; enforced flag = the attestation/locked-down architecture A disowned) was never escaped. A asserted a middle path (household-verified managed account with store/API conditions) but never reconciled novelty with feasibility, and B's follow-ups—the browser-as-highway dilemma, the borrowed-login-in-thirty-seconds turn, and the server-side point—kept closing the exits. A's car analogy was cleanly double-turned (a car restricts a machine, not information; the abused teen's recourse arrives through the very device being sealed). A's clipped Rebuttal 2 was a real execution cost, and A's closing reasserted rather than resolved, leaving the status-quo wedge and attestation squeeze unanswered. B answered both pressure questions directly with concrete household-level alternatives and sharp A1/A2 structure. Both sides were disciplined and well-written, but B controlled the central clash from Rebuttal 1 onward and made the decision easy.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1: "Everything PRO defends already exists... the proposition adds exactly one thing: that apps cannot easily bypass"—then catching A's shuffle by quoting A's own "suggestion competing with a business model" line against A's managed-minor flag, showing A's enforcement mechanism (refuse unsigned clients, block sideloads) is the very cage A called rhetoric. A never recovered from this wedge.</best_rebuttal>
